questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
questions.explanation: Binary search eliminates half the elements with each comparison. After k comparisons, n/2^k elements remain, so k = log n.

questions.question: What is the SPACE complexity of quicksort?
options: O(log n) - average case call stack
O(log n) average, O(n) worst case
questions.explanation: Quicksort is in-place but uses O(log n) stack space on average (balanced partitions) or O(n) in worst case (already sorted, bad pivot). Tail recursion optimization can reduce this.

questions.question: What is the amortized time complexity of appending n elements to a dynamic array?
questions.explanation: While individual appends may trigger O(n) resizing, the amortized cost per append is O(1). Total for n appends is O(n).

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of the following code?
result = ""
for char in s:
    result += char
questions.explanation: String concatenation creates a new string each time. For a string of length n, each concatenation copies all previous characters. Total: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = O(n²).

questions.question: What is the SPACE complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci fib(n)?
questions.explanation: The TIME is O(2^n), but SPACE is O(n) because the maximum call stack depth is n. When one branch completes, its stack frames are reclaimed before exploring other branches.

questions.question: For the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), what is the time complexity?
questions.explanation: Using Master Theorem: a=2, b=2, d=1. Since d = log_b(a) = 1, the result is O(n^d log n) = O(n log n). This is the recurrence for merge sort.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of hash table lookup?
questions.explanation: Worst case O(n) occurs when all keys hash to the same bucket, creating a long chain. Average case with good hash function is O(1).

questions.question: Why is building a heap from n elements O(n) instead of O(n log n)?
options: Because half the nodes are leaves requiring no work, and sift-down costs decrease geometrically
Because we use a faster algorithm than inserting n times
It's actually O(n log n), O(n) is a common misconception
questions.explanation: Half the nodes are leaves (0 sift-down). 1/4 sift down 1 level, 1/8 sift down 2 levels, etc. The sum n×(1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8 + ...) converges to O(n).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap?
questions.explanation: Each vertex is extracted once (V extractions × log V each). Each edge may trigger a decrease-key (E updates × log V each). Total: O((V + E) log V).

questions.question: A function runs a loop from 1 to n, and inside each iteration calls a O(log n) function. What is the total time complexity?
questions.explanation: n iterations × O(log n) per iteration = O(n log n). You multiply when operations are nested.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.explanation: BFS visits each vertex once (O(V)) and examines each edge once (O(E)). Total: O(V + E).

questions.question: You have an algorithm with O(n²) time and O(1) space. Your colleague proposes O(n) time with O(n) space. Which statement is true?
options: The O(n) time version is always better
The O(n²) version is always better due to space efficiency
It depends on the constraints - time vs memory tradeoff
questions.explanation: This is a classic space-time tradeoff. If memory is constrained or n is small, O(n²) time with O(1) space may be preferable. For large n with available memory, O(n) time is better.
